title: The First Morning
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 33 of 40
content:
The first morning I woke beside Severus Snape, he was already awake.

Of course he was.

He lay on his back staring at the ceiling with the expression of a man conducting a hostile review of existence.

I blinked at him.

“Good morning.”

His eyes moved toward me.

“Debatable.”

I smiled into the pillow.

We had spent the night at Spinner's End.

Not accidentally.

Not because a storm trapped us or the Floo failed or some emergency made privacy convenient.

We had chosen it.

That distinction mattered enough for Snape to ask once more if I was comfortable. I said yes, and he closed the bedroom door.

We kissed, talked through the pauses, and laughed when we both reached for the teapot at once. When we were ready to be alone, the rest of the night belonged to us.

We had gone slowly.

We had stopped once.

We had started again because we both wanted to.

Now morning made everything ordinary in the most alarming way.

His hair was everywhere.

One side had flattened against the pillow. The other stood at an angle I had never seen in public.

I stared.

“No,” he said.

I laughed.

“You look—”

“Finish that sentence carefully.”

“Human.”

His eyes narrowed.

“Disappointing, I know.”

“Profoundly.”

I moved closer.

He went still for the smallest second before relaxing.

Morning touch, I realized, was new territory.

Last night every contact had been asked in explicit language.

Now I let my hand rest on the blanket between us.

“Can I?”

His gaze dropped to it.

“Yes.”

I touched his shoulder.

Then his chest.

Nothing sexual.

Just warm skin and the rhythm of his breathing beneath my palm.

His hand covered mine.

“This is strange,” he said.

“What is?”

“You being here.”

“Bad strange?”

He considered.

“No.”

“Good strange?”

“Do not make me use that phrase.”

“Neutral strange?”

“Unfamiliar.”

That was more honest.

I nodded.

“Me too.”

His eyebrows rose.

“What?”

“You appear comfortable.”

“I am performing competence.”

His mouth curved.

“Recognizable technique.”

In the morning, we stayed beneath the blankets longer than either of us usually allowed ourselves, then made tea before facing the day.

Snape pretended this was because the room was cold.

I pretended to believe him.

Eventually the kettle downstairs whistled on a timing charm.

He closed his eyes.

“You enchanted the kettle?”

“Yes.”

“For what time?”

“Seven.”

I looked at the clock.

“It is seven.”

“I am aware.”

“You planned morning tea.”

“I plan most things.”

“Romantic.”

He pulled the blanket over his face.

I laughed so hard I had to sit up.

“This relationship is intolerable,” he said from beneath the blanket.

“You're hiding.”

“I am reconsidering.”

“Agreement two. No disappearing as strategy.”

The blanket lowered.

His eyes were amused.

“I hate that document.”

“You wrote half of it.”

“An error.”

We went downstairs.

The kitchen was cold, but sunlight reached the table. Snape brewed tea. I found bread and eggs. He objected to my method of cooking eggs.

“You are stirring too aggressively.”

“They are eggs.”

“Texture remains relevant.”

“You're not allowed to turn breakfast into Potions.”

“Everything involving heat, timing, and ingredients has standards.”

“Should I use a silver cauldron?”

“Do not be ridiculous. Copper would distribute heat better.”

I stared.

He stared back.

Then we both started laughing.

It was absurdly domestic.

That frightened me a little.

I realized it while buttering toast.

The feeling must have crossed my face because Snape stopped criticizing the eggs.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

His eyebrow rose.

I sighed.

“This is nice.”

His expression became wary.

“Yes.”

“And nice can become expected.”

He waited.

“And expected can become required.”

Understanding moved through his face.

“You are afraid of obligation.”

“Sometimes.”

“Of me?”

“Not exactly.”

He set down his cup.

“Explain exactly.”

I smiled faintly.

“You really hate ambiguity.”

“Yes.”

I leaned against the counter.

“I don't want waking up here to become something either of us has to do to prove we're serious.”

Snape considered.

“No.”

“No?”

“It will not.”

“That simple?”

“Yes.”

He picked up his cup.

I stared.

“You're good at this sometimes.”

“Do not spread the rumor.”

Warmth returned.

I put the eggs on plates.

Snape tasted them.

“Well?”

He chewed with maddening deliberation.

“Acceptable.”

I threw a napkin at him.

He caught it.

After breakfast, we dressed.

Snape's shirt collar caught against the scar on his throat. He hissed and pulled it away.

I watched his hand tremble.

“Help?” I asked.

A pause.

“Yes.”

I stepped close.

He stood still while I fastened the top buttons more loosely and folded the collar so it did not rub.

My fingers moved near the scar without touching it.

His breathing stayed even.

“Better?”

“Yes.”

I smoothed the fabric once over his shoulder.

He looked at me.

“You are staring.”

“I like you.”

“That is not a defense.”

“I love you.”

His face immediately betrayed him.

Color.

Softness.

Annoyance at both.

“That is even less relevant.”

“I disagree.”

He kissed my forehead.

Quickly, as if hoping to escape consequences.

I caught his coat before he could step away.

“Again.”

His eyebrow rose.

“Demanding.”

“Yes.”

He kissed me properly.

When we finally left the house, he locked the door and stood on the pavement beside me.

“Tonight?” he asked.

Not an expectation.

A question.

I thought about my own room at Hogwarts, my work, the pleasure of missing someone by choice rather than obligation.

“Tomorrow,” I said.

Snape nodded.

“Tomorrow.”

No hurt.

No punishment.

Just a plan.

The first morning did not turn us into one person.

It gave us breakfast, bad hair, careful questions, and a door we could leave separately.

For me, that was more romantic than destiny.\n\nWe ate breakfast at the small table by the window.\n\nSnape had toast. I had tea strong enough to qualify as disciplinary action. Neither of us commented on the fact that he had remembered exactly how I took it.\n\nFor several minutes, the most intimate thing in the room was butter.\n\nI liked that.\n\nIt gave the night before somewhere ordinary to land.\n\nSnape opened the newspaper, read two paragraphs, and lowered it again.\n\n“You are watching me.”\n\n“You're holding the paper upside down.”\n\nHe looked at it.\n\nTurned it around.\n\n“I was testing the print quality.”\n\n“Obviously.”\n\n“Do not become smug before nine.”\n\n“What time is smugness permitted?”\n\n“Never. I was attempting compromise.”\n\nI laughed, and some of the remaining tension left his shoulders.\n\nThat was when I understood that he was waiting for the bill.\n\nNot money. Meaning. Expectation. The invisible invoice people sometimes handed each other after vulnerability: I gave you this, therefore you owe me that.\n\nI set my cup down.\n\n“Nothing changed that I didn't agree to change.”\n\nHis eyes lifted.\n\n“Explain.”\n\n“You don't owe me more access because we were close last night. I don't get to decide we're inseparable because I woke up here. You still get doors. I still get mine.”\n\nHis face went very still.\n\n“And if I want you here again?”\n\n“Ask.”\n\n“That simple.”\n\n“Yes.”\n\nHe looked irritated by the answer, which meant it had probably reached something important.\n\n“And if you do not?” he asked.\n\n“I'll say no.”\n\nHis mouth tightened.\n\n“Not because I don't care about you,” I added. “Because I want yes to mean yes when I say it.”\n\nA long silence.\n\nThen Snape nodded.\n\n“Reasonable.”\n\n“Write down the date.”\n\n“Do not ruin it.”\n\nI grinned.\n\nWe finished breakfast.\n\nAfterward, Snape gathered the plates before I could. He carried them to the sink with the stiff concentration of a man who had survived a war and remained suspicious of domestic labor.\n\n“You can use magic,” I said.\n\n“I am aware.”\n\n“You are washing a plate by hand.”\n\n“The spell left residue yesterday.”\n\n“That is the most Severus Snape explanation possible.”\n\nHe ignored me.\n\nI dried the plate he handed over.\n\nThat became the shape of the morning: nothing dramatic, everything slightly new. He made a list for the laboratory. I corrected his list because he had forgotten food. He added coffee under protest. I added a second line that said ACTUAL FOOD. He crossed it out. I wrote it again.\n\nBy ten we were arguing about a sleeping draught formula that had been used on injured veterans because it suppressed dreams too aggressively.\n\n“The memories return on waking with increased disorientation,” I said.\n\n“I know.”\n\n“Then why are we keeping the standard concentration?”\n\n“We are not.”\n\nI looked at him.\n\nSnape slid a notebook across the table. The page contained three alternate ratios and a list of possible stabilizers.\n\n“You've already been working on it.”\n\n“For six weeks.”\n\n“And you were going to tell me when?”\n\n“When you stopped asking irritating questions.”\n\n“So never.”\n\n“Precisely.”\n\nI read the notes again.\n\nThe problem was difficult. Not impossible. More importantly, it mattered to him for reasons he would not say aloud.\n\nWar had left too many people unable to sleep.\n\nSnape knew something about that.\n\nI closed the notebook. “All right.”\n\n“All right what?”\n\n“Let's make something better.”\n\nHis expression shifted.\n\nNot softer exactly.\n\nLess alone.\n\n“After breakfast?” he asked dryly.\n\nI held up the clean plate. “Apparently we're very domestic now.”\n\n“God help us.”\n\nThe laboratory waited downstairs.\n\nSo did the problem he could not solve alone.
